lesson_title: Monoxide or Dioxide: The Prefix That Can Save Your Life
hook_text: Carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide differ by one prefix. One you breathe out. The other kills.
clip_script: Chemists name compounds with a code. Metal plus non-metal: the metal keeps its name, the non-metal gets -ide. Sodium and chlorine, sodium chloride. Magnesium and oxygen, magnesium oxide. But two non-metals can join in different ways, so the name has to count, in Greek. Mono, one. Di, two. Tri, three. Tetra, four. Carbon with one oxygen: carbon monoxide, CO. Carbon with two oxygens: carbon dioxide, CO2. One prefix apart. Carbon dioxide is what you breathe out and what makes cold drinks fizz. Carbon monoxide comes from a brazier or generator burning in a closed room, has no colour and no smell, and quietly stops your blood carrying oxygen. Sulfur dioxide, SO2, is the choking smell of burning coal; sulfur trioxide, SO3, turns into acid in rain. Two tiny rules: never start with mono, and drop the doubled vowel, so it is monoxide, not mono-oxide. The name is the formula, in words.
visual_style: Name tags snap onto ball-and-stick molecules; Greek prefixes count up on fingers; a CO molecule glows red with a warning icon beside a brazier while a CO2 molecule bubbles out of a cold drink.
pacing: Quick rule beats, a counting rhythm on the prefixes, a serious pause on carbon monoxide, a neat closing line.
